title: Temple jewellery: designs, motifs and how to wear it
description: A guide to South Indian temple jewellery: what the classic motifs mean, the key pieces from kasu mala to vanki, and how to wear temple designs today.
intro: Temple jewellery is the heavy, gold-toned style from South India that takes its designs from temple art: goddesses, peacocks, lotuses and coins. It is traditionally linked to the jewellery once made to adorn deities, and it later became the signature look of classical dancers and South Indian brides. Today you can wear it with a silk saree for a wedding or as a single statement piece with something much simpler.

sections.heading: Where the style comes from
paragraphs: The name says it all. Ornaments made for temple deities were rich in religious imagery, and over time similar designs came to be worn by people, especially Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi dancers, whose stage jewellery still follows this style closely.

Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh each have their own variations, and Nagercoil in Tamil Nadu is often mentioned as a well-known centre for temple-style work. Traditionally the pieces were made in gold and set with red and green stones; today much of what is sold is gold-plated or antique-finish fashion jewellery that keeps the designs alive at a lower cost.

sections.heading: Common motifs and what they represent
paragraphs: Meanings can vary by community and family, but these motifs come up again and again:
list: Goddess Lakshmi: the most popular figure, associated with prosperity, often seated on a lotus in the centre pendant.
Peacock: linked to beauty and grace, and associated with Lord Murugan in many South Indian traditions.
Lotus: a symbol of purity, used in pendants, studs and borders.
Mango (manga): a sign of fertility and abundance, the base of the famous manga mala.
Coins (kasu): small coin shapes, usually stamped with Lakshmi, strung together into a necklace.
Annam (swan) and elephants: seen in borders, jhumkas and waist belts.

sections.heading: The key pieces in a temple set
paragraphs: A full traditional bridal look can include many pieces, but you rarely need all of them. Here is what each one is:

The kasu mala is the coin necklace, usually long. The manga mala uses mango-shaped links. The attigai is a choker that sits close to the neck. Jhumkas are bell-shaped earrings, often with a mattal, an ear chain that runs up into the hair. The nethi chutti is the forehead ornament, the vanki is an armlet worn on the upper arm, and the oddiyanam is a waist belt that holds the saree pleats in place.

If you are building a collection slowly, start with the two pieces you will wear most: a pair of temple jhumkas and one medium-length Lakshmi or coin necklace. Together they cover festivals, family functions and a guest look at weddings. Add a choker, waist belt or vanki later, only if you have a bridal or dance occasion that calls for the full set. This way, nothing sits unworn in the cupboard.

sections.heading: How to wear temple jewellery as a bride
paragraphs: Temple jewellery is made for Kanjeevaram and other heavy silk sarees. The trick is layering by length: a choker or short necklace at the neck, a medium Lakshmi pendant necklace, and a long kasu or manga mala that falls towards the waist. Keep the earrings large to balance the necklace.

If your saree has a lot of zari, choose temple pieces with an antique or matte finish so the jewellery does not compete with the fabric. Bright yellow gold-tone works best when the saree is a strong single colour like maroon, mustard or green. For more bridal inspiration across styles, browse Varaha's [bridal jewellery](/women/bridal-jewellery) looks.

sections.heading: Wearing it outside weddings
paragraphs: Temple jewellery does not have to come out only for big functions. A few easy ways to wear it:
list: One long coin necklace over a plain cotton or handloom saree for a festival or office puja.
Temple jhumkas alone with a solid kurta, hair in a low bun.
A Lakshmi pendant on a simple chain with a black or white blouse for a fusion look.
A temple choker with a plain silk blouse and contrasting skirt for a concert or naming ceremony.

sections.heading: Buying and caring for fashion temple jewellery
paragraphs: Look closely at the figure work. In a good piece, the goddess's face, the peacock feathers and the coin stamps are crisp, not blurred. Check that stones sit firmly and that the back is finished smoothly. After wearing, wipe the piece dry, especially where it touched skin, and store it in a separate pouch. Antique finishes hide wear well, but they still dislike water and perfume.

Long temple necklaces can tangle with the hooks of other pieces, so lay them flat in a box rather than coiling them in a pouch. Wrap figure-work pendants in tissue, since the raised faces and edges are the first places plating rubs thin.

faq.q: What is temple jewellery made of?
faq.a: Traditionally gold, often with red and green stones. Most temple jewellery sold today is gold-plated brass or alloy, often with an antique finish.

faq.q: Can North Indian brides wear temple jewellery?
faq.a: Yes. Many brides choose a temple necklace or jhumkas for a South Indian ceremony, reception or a silk saree look.
A necklace made of small coin-shaped pieces, usually stamped with Goddess Lakshmi, traditionally associated with prosperity.

faq.q: Is temple jewellery only for sarees?
faq.a: No. Single pieces like jhumkas or a pendant work well with kurtas, lehengas and even fusion outfits.
